query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: During elevated-temperature exposure, degradation of the additively manufactured fcc Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy is governed by oxygen transport along grain boundaries leading to distinct oxidation processes: in oxidizing atmospheres, rapid grain boundary oxidation forms brittle, continuous oxide films (e.g., Cr2O3 and/or TiO2) that weaken intergranular cohesion and spur crack initiation and spallation, whereas in reducing environments the absence of a robust, protective oxide allows oxygen to ingress internally, forming detrimental oxide precipitates that destabilize the matrix—both pathways ultimately leading to catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built additive manufactured alloy with a homogeneous, fine-grained fcc microstructure, possessing a thin native oxide layer.
generation.intervention: A controlled change in the ambient gas chemistry during high-temperature exposure by varying the oxygen partial pressure; specifically comparing a well‐defined oxidizing environment (with higher O2 partial pressure) against a reducing environment (with low oxygen and possible addition of H2 or CO as reducing agents).
generation.conditions: Exposure at elevated temperatures (approximately 700–900 °C) for fixed durations under precisely controlled oxidizing and reducing gas atmospheres.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries and the distribution/formation of oxide phases along these boundaries and within the matrix.
generation.mechanism: Oxygen diffusing rapidly along grain boundaries in oxidizing conditions reacts with reactive alloying elements (e.g., Cr, Ti) to form continuous and brittle oxide layers that reduce intergranular cohesion and lead to early crack formation and spallation. In reducing conditions, the lack of an effective passivating oxide film permits deeper oxygen penetration and internal oxidation that results in the formation of discrete oxide precipitates, destabilizing the fcc matrix and enhancing the propensity for catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline state, specimens exposed to a higher oxygen partial pressure will develop thicker and more continuous intergranular oxide films accompanied by reduced mechanical integrity (evidenced by lower fracture toughness), whereas those in a reducing atmosphere will show more dispersed internal oxide precipitates and similar degradation in mechanical performance; both degraded states will correlate with a measurable reduction in structural and mechanical performance before catastrophic failure.
generation.baseline: The as-built alloy exhibits a fine, homogeneous fcc microstructure with minimal oxide formation and maintains its mechanical integrity under ambient conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under high-temperature exposures (700–900 °C) and for exposure durations of several hours where oxygen diffusion and reaction kinetics become significant; outside these temperature or time regimes, alternative degradation mechanisms may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: The precise oxide composition, kinetics of oxidation, and the relative contribution of each pathway may be influenced by local microstructural variations originating from additive manufacturing. Additionally, minor element segregation and residual stresses could modify the oxidation behavior, introducing some uncertainty in the exact critical thresholds for catastrophic failure.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical sets of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy specimens and expose one set to a controlled oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., defined O2 partial pressure) and another to a reducing atmosphere (e.g., low O2 with H2 or CO additives) at 700–900 °C for a fixed time. Post-exposure, analyze microstructural changes using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and X-ray diffraction (XRD), and perform mechanical tests (e.g., fracture toughness, hardness, and tensile tests).
measurements: Grain boundary oxide thickness and continuity (via SEM/TEM)
Phase identification and spatial distribution of oxides (via XRD/EDS)
Mechanical property degradation (fracture toughness, tensile strength, hardness)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the analysis shows that the oxidation morphology, i.e., both oxide thickness and distribution, does not significantly differ between the oxidizing and reducing conditions—or if the differences observed do not correlate with a corresponding and differential degradation in the mechanical properties—the proposed mechanism (differential oxidation pathways governing degradation and catastrophic failure) is falsified.
